paper_title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at https://github.com/lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Machine learning models for spacecraft navigation are trained almost entirely on the output of simulator, then deployed against physical system that the simulator only approximates. Real images of target spacecraft in orbit, labelled with its pose, essentially do not exist. Estimators therefore learn from rendered images and meet real ones for the first time during the mission. The SPEED+ benchmark [20] was built to make that discrepancy measurable. It pairs 60,000 labelled synthetic training images of the Tango spacecraft with 9,500 real images of physical mockup, lit two ways: lightbox, diffuse light like Earth albedo, and sunlamp, collimated solar simulator that gives harsh directional light. On its predecessor SPEED, whose real test images show the same mockup, the top ten entries of the 2019 challenge degraded 2.740 in pose score from synthetic to real images (Table 1: winner 40, runner-up 5.3, median 8.5) [12]. Preprint. SPEED+s synthetic images do not come from physics simulation. They are rendered by an OpenGL rasteriser, the Optical Stimulator camera emulator, which shades sunlit foil and metal with an empirical formula chosen for speed rather than fidelity [20]. That formula stands in for the physics of light that the renderer never computes, much as climate model uses simple rules for the clouds it cannot resolve, and it is where the simulators error lives. The error is therefore radiometric rather than geometric: ranges and pose distributions match across domains, and only appearance differs. Real mylar and machined metal reflect specularly, and collimated lamp turns those reflections into hard shadow edges and saturated pixels. Saturation is not shading error at all but happens in the cameras detector, which means the simulator gets the camera wrong as well as the scene. In these terms photometric augmentation stack is discrepancy model, an unvalidated guess at how simulator and reality differ. It does not correct the simulator but spreads the training images across the differences it guesses at. This paper is about what happens when that guess is wrong: the model loses accuracy, and it also loses its calibration without any outward sign. We use SPEED+ as controlled testbed and ask what actually transfers from simulation to reality. Our estimator is direct-regression baseline, an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 with small head. We train it on synthetic images alone, in 22 design of {backbone frozen, last stage trained} {no augmentation, photometric augmentation}, and evaluate it on the full lightbox and sunlamp test sets. Every arm runs on three seeds (for the frozen un-augmented arm, two of them retrain only the head), and checkpoints are selected on synthetic validation images only. Our contributions: The model does not know it is failing. Split-conformal regions calibrated to 90% on held-out synthetic data keep that coverage in-domain. On sunlamp they cover only 915% of rotation errors, and test-time BatchNorm adaptation lifts that only to 1120%. On the weakest arms the attitude cone spans roughly half of all orientations, which keeps it valid but makes it meaningless. Transfer is asymmetric. With the backbone frozen, scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad, but sunlamp only from 2.04 to 1.99 rad, less than twice its seed s.d., and the same holds for either factor alone. Training layer 4 took synthetic error further, from 1.03 to 0.32 rad, and 6383% of that extra gain carried across: lightbox went from 1.76 to 1.17 rad and sunlamp from 1.99 to 1.53. Augmentation is directional. We built our photometric stack in good faith to anticipate harsh real illumination, yet it models neither real domain well, and the diffuse lightbox markedly less badly  (Fig. 2)  . With layer 4 adapting, it improved lightbox by 0.18 rad on every seed while sunlamp moved no further than seed-to-seed variation, and with the backbone frozen the order reverses. Removing blur, noise and the glare blob does not resolve sunlamp either. The revision is pre-registered and auditable. Every experiment added after review had its prediction and decision rule committed before its result was opened, and five of those rules softened or qualified claim of the workshop submission (App. H). The per-image predictions are public, and so is script that checks every number in this paper against the released results. This extended version adds what the workshops five-page limit left out. Section 2 places the study among prior work, including the 2019 challenges per-entry results, and Sec. 4 reports what it took to get baseline worth testing. The post-review experiments move from the appendix into the body, and every arm now has three seeds. Section 7 shows what the real-domain failures look like, Sec. 8 brings together the results on normalisation statistics, and Sec. 9 adds coverage by range. Appendices EH give the per-checkpoint analyses, the reproducibility details and the full pre-registration record.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Prior work on spacecraft pose has measured how far methods fall across the synthetic-to-real gap. We hold one simple method fixed and ask different question: which of its gains cross the gap, and does its uncertainty survive it? Spacecraft pose benchmarks and the gap. SPEED and its 2019 challenge [12] set up the problem: synthetic training images, and real test images of Tango mockup. The top ten entries degraded 2.740 from synthetic to real  (Table 1)  . The runner-up, EPFL_cvlab, had the best real score, and the best entry without PnP, pedro_fairspace, finished third. SPEED+ [20] made the gap itself the object of study, with two real domains, one lit diffusely and one by collimated sun simulator, and SPEC2021 [21] reports the competition held on them. SPNv2 [18], the reference method on SPEED+, 2 combines multi-task representations with heavy style augmentation, the texture randomisation that Park et al. [19] first used with keypoints and PnP. Direct methods map an image straight to pose, as PoseNet [11] did for camera relocalisation and SPN [24] and URSO [22] did for spacecraft. Keypoint pipelines instead regress 2D landmarks and solve for the pose geometrically. The 2019 winner [2] regressed landmark heatmaps and refined the pose by nonlinear optimisation, and keypoint methods took the top two places, but the ranking was on synthetic data. On real data the 2019 results do not separate the two classes: PnP entries in the top ten degraded 4.840, the others 2.724. For regression the rotation representation matters too, since quaternions cover SO(3) twice and every rotation representation in four or fewer dimensions is discontinuous [32]. We keep the quaternion and remove the sign ambiguity instead (Sec. 3). Sim-to-real for vision. Domain randomisation [27, 28] varies rendering so widely that the real world looks like one more variation, and style augmentation [10] randomises texture and colour by style transfer. Our photometric stack is the cheap end of the same idea, and its blur and noise are standard corruptions [9]. Test-time adaptation of BatchNorm statistics [14, 23, 16] uses unlabelled target images, as does adversarial domain adaptation [6], and we test the first (Sec. 8) but not the second. Across many models and shifts, out-of-distribution accuracy is often close to linear function of in-distribution accuracy [15], and robustness beyond that line is rare [25], question Figure 1 asks of our configurations. Uncertainty under shift. Split conformal prediction [30, 13, 1] guarantees coverage in finite samples, on average over test points, as long as calibration and test data are exchangeable, which is exactly what synthetic-to-real shift breaks. Two extensions relax the assumption, but neither fits here. Weighted conformal prediction [26] restores validity under covariate shift given the likelihood ratio between domains, which needs domains that overlap. Adaptive conformal inference [7] tracks coverage online from feedback on its own errors, and navigator in orbit has no labels to give that feedback. Coverage conditional on feature such as range is attainable only in weaker forms [29, 5], so we measure it (Sec. 9) rather than guarantee it. Predictive uncertainty is known to degrade under dataset shift [17], and conformal prediction has been carried to object pose through keypoints [31]. We measure what synthetic calibration is worth on real images.

sections.title: 3 Setup
sections.content: Data. From SPEED+s synthetic domain we sample 28,000 training images from the official training labels and 2,000 validation images from the official validation set, and downscale them to 320512 grayscale to fit the GPU available. The conformal analysis (Sec. 9) draws two more disjoint sets of 1,000 from the official validation set, excluding those 2,000: one to calibrate on and one to test in-domain. Both real domains serve in full as test sets, lightbox (6,740 images) and sunlamp (2,791), and no real image influences training, tuning or model selection. Range distributions match across domains, so any extra difficulty on the real images comes from appearance, not from harder poses. 3 Model and loss. ResNet-50 [8] pretrained on ImageNet [4] feeds its global-average-pooled 2048d features to two-layer MLP head. The head regresses translation (targets z-scored per component) and unit quaternion q: direct pose regression [11, 24, 22]. The loss treats the two separately, = MSE(ˆt, t) + λ (1 ˆq, q2), with λ=1 and ˆq ℓ2-normalised. Because and encode the same rotation, naive quaternion MSE gives the network contradictory targets [32]. Two choices remove that ambiguity: the squared inner product ignores sign, and the labels are canonicalised to one hemisphere. Section 4 shows what it cost us to find this out. In the two frozen arms the backbone runs in inference mode and keeps its ImageNet The 22 arms. BatchNorm statistics, so only the head is trained. In the two layer-4 arms the final ResNet stage is trained as well, so its BatchNorm statistics follow the (augmented) synthetic training images. All arms share one configuration: Adam, learning rate 103, batch 16 and 20 epochs, with checkpoint every second epoch. Each arm keeps the checkpoint with the best synthetic validation rotation error, and each runs on seeds 42, 43 and 44. frozen backbone without augmentation sees the same inputs in every epoch, so its pooled features can be computed once and cached, and seeds 43 and 44 of that arm retrain the head on the cache. As check, the published seed-42 head applied to the cache reproduces its errors to within 0.0005 rad (App. D). Augmentation. The photometric factor is good-faith attempt to anticipate harsh real illumination. It jitters brightness (0.651.5) and contrast (0.5), applies log-uniform gamma in [0.5, 2], and adds soft, clamped Gaussian sun glare blob (σ [10, 50] px), Gaussian blur and additive Gaussian noise, each stochastic component with p=0.5, followed by random erasing. Table 2 gives every parameter, and Sec. 6 examines what the stack actually prepares the model for. Table 2: The photometric stack, in order. Stochastic components apply with p=0.5. Arm drops blur and noise, and arm also drops the glare blob.

sections.title: 4 Getting an honest baseline
sections.content: Before the gap can be measured, the in-domain error has to mean what it says. Two problems stood between our first model and that, and neither was sim-to-real effect  (Table 3)  . The double cover. Our first model regressed all seven pose targets, z-scored, with plain MSE. quaternion and its negative encode the same rotation, so near-identical images can carry targets on opposite sides of the sphere, and MSE pulls the prediction towards their average: the dataset mean [32]. After 50 epochs on 4,000 images the training loss was still 0.892, barely below the 1.0 that predicting the mean of z-scored targets scores. Canonicalising the labels to one hemisphere, with nothing else changed, brought the training loss to 0.285 and the validation rotation error to 1.666 rad. This bug would appear even if no real image existed, because it belongs to the labels rather than to the shift. Memorisation. The next step scaled to 28,000 images and pooled 2048-d features. The first such run (seed 42) scores 0.654 rad on its own training images, 0.40 rad better than on validation. Those 0.40 rad are generalisation gap, and the rest of its validation error is what head on frozen ImageNet features can fit at all. More data attacks the first part, and adapting the backbone the second. One lesson carries beyond this study: take bundled change apart before crediting any piece of it, as Section 5 does for data and features. sections.title: 6 Augmentation is directional once the backbone adapts
sections.content: Which way augmentation helps depends on the backbone it trains. With layer 4 adapting, the stack improves the diffuse domain it models and leaves sunlamp unresolved, but with the backbone frozen the order reverses. Seeds are paired across arms (42, 43 and 44 in both), so we read per-seed differences rather than comparing spreads. On lightbox, augmentation lowers the error on every seed: 0.183, 0.185 and 0.170 rad, about 15% each time, and the mean moves from 1.166 0.018 to 0.987 0.010 rad. On sunlamp the paired differences change sign: +0.116, 0.265 and 0.047 rad (1.534 0.075 1.468 0.119), spread wider than the effect it would have to establish. Translation is weaker indicator, but it points the same way  (Table 4)  . Lightbox improves within noise, while on sunlamp two of the three augmented seeds (0.405, 0.399) fail to beat the fitted constants 0.372, so augmentation pushes sunlamp translation to the no-skill line. With layer 4 adapting, the lightbox gain does not come at the cost of the synthetic reference, whose error is essentially unchanged (0.317 0.322 rad). We report absolute error rather than the synthetic-to-real gap, because gap can narrow merely because the reference gets worse. With the backbone frozen, that is what happens: augmentation worsens synthetic error on every seed (by 0.1340.169 rad, paired against the head-only retrains in Table 6). There the direction also reverses: sunlamp improves on every seed (0.069 to 0.132 rad), and by more than lightbox (0.012 to 0.117), so augmentation favours lightbox only once layer 4 adapts. sections.title: 7 What the failures look like
sections.content: The real-domain failures are broad rather than discrete confusions. pose estimator can fail in two quite different ways: it can mistake an object for symmetric copy of itself, which piles up errors near π, or it can spread its errors widely, and we pre-registered tests for both (App. H). Neither real domain is bimodal  (Fig. 3)  : on every layer-4 checkpoint the share of errors within 0.3 rad of π is 0.030.05 on lightbox and 0.070.10 on sunlamp, below the 0.19 that uniform guessing puts there. Nor do the near-π errors share an axis. symmetry flip would concentrate their axes in the body frame, but the share within 20 of the principal axis reaches the pre-registered 0.18 on only two of six checkpoints per domain, and an in-plane confusion would concentrate them in the camera frame, where the share reaches 0.18 on none  (Table 16)  . Lightbox errors peak near π/8 (medians 0.690.92 rad). Sunlamp errors spread from there towards π (medians 1.111.54), with long tail that stays below the uniform density beyond about π/2. Under harsh light, then, the model is not mistaking Tango for flipped copy of itself: its errors are simply broad, even though its stated confidence says otherwise (Sec. 9). 8 Figure 3: Rotation-error densities on each domain for the layer-4 arms, pooled over three seeds, against the density uniform guessing gives, (1 cos θ)/π (dotted).

sections.title: 8 Normalisation statistics
sections.content: The layer-4 arms differ from the frozen ones in two ways at once: layer 4s weights adapt, and so do its BatchNorm statistics, which then follow the augmented synthetic images. The three results below pull these two changes apart. First, statistics alone do not explain the layer-4 gain, since re-estimating every BatchNorm layer of the frozen backbone on synthetic images, weights untouched, makes its head worse on every domain: 1.394 rad on synthetic, 2.064 on lightbox and 2.107 on sunlamp, against 1.030, 1.761 and 1.986 with ImageNet statistics  (Table 5)  . Second, the direction augmentation pushes in depends on whether layer 4, and with it its statistics, adapts. With the backbone frozen, augmentation helps sunlamp more than lightbox on every seed, but once layer 4 adapts it helps lightbox on every seed and leaves sunlamp unresolved  (Table 6)  . Third, swapping in real-domain statistics at test time helps accuracy but not calibration. AdaBN [14] re-estimates layer 4s statistics on unlabelled images from one half of each real domain, and we test on the other half. It lowers rotation error on every layer-4 checkpoint, by 0.09 rad on lightbox and 0.16 on sunlamp on average, yet rotation coverage reaches only 2440% and 1120%  (Table 9)  . sections.title: 9 The model does not know it is failing
sections.content: Does the estimators uncertainty survive the shift? For each arm we calibrate split-conformal regions [30, 13, 1] on 1,000 fresh synthetic images, used neither for training nor for checkpoint selection. For translation the score is the error in metres, which gives keep-out sphere, and for rotation it is the geodesic angle, which gives cone, both at nominal 90% with the finite-samplecorrected quantile. In-domain, the regions work: test coverage is close to nominal for every arm and metric (87.791.4%), and its ClopperPearson [3] interval includes 90% in every case but one, the frozen un-augmented arms translation (87.7%, 85.589.7%), which is slightly anti-conservative. On the real domains coverage collapses  (Table 10)  : for the layer-4 arm without augmentation, over its three seeds, rotation coverage is 913% on sunlamp and 2127% on lightbox (translation 1418% and 3335%), and App. gives every arm, domain and seed, with intervals and inflation factors. To restore 90% rotation coverage on sunlamp, that arms attitude cone would have to grow 56, from 0.5 to 2.8 rad, into cone holding roughly 78% of all orientations.2 Coverage follows the directional finding of Sec. 6: augmentation raises lightbox rotation coverage to 3338%, but sunlamp only to 1315%. The frozen arms fail the opposite way, because their 90% attitude cone already spans 2.162.42 rad, or 4256% of all possible orientations, which keeps it valid in-domain but makes it too wide to navigate by. navigation filter fed these poses in deployment would receive wrong inputs that look exactly as confident as correct ones  (Fig. 4)  . Test-time adaptation does not rescue this (Sec. 8): AdaBN lowers the error, but lifts rotation coverage only to 2440% on lightbox and 1120% on sunlamp. sections.title: 10 Discussion and limitations
sections.content: Ratios flatter weak models. degradation ratio divides by the in-domain error. On sunlamp, even the skill-free constant pose (App. C) scores only 7.3 our synthetic S, so our modest ratio does not mean small gap. Nor do the 2019 results separate method classes: PnP entries in the top ten degraded 4.840, the others 2.724  (Table 1)  . SPNv2 [18], the reference sim-to-real method on SPEED+, closes far more of the gap with multi-task representations and heavy style augmentation. We do not compete with it but characterise how gains transfer under simple estimator. Limitations. In the frozen un-augmented arm, seed 42 was trained end to end and seeds 43 and 44 retrain only the head on cached features. With the backbone frozen the two compute the same thing, but they draw different random numbers and ran on different hardware: when retrained head-only for comparison, seed 42 moves by 0.04 rad on synthetic and 0.06 on sunlamp, about as far as one seed from another. The difference is negligible, but we state it because the frozen cell of Table 4 combines the two. The ablation arms and two frozen augmented seeds ran on different hardware from the published runs. Sunlamp is also the smaller test set (2,791 images), and three seeds do not resolve sunlamp effects of 0.1 rad. We study one estimator on one benchmark at 320512, and with real-domain errors near 1 rad it is diagnostic baseline rather than deployable navigator. Our directionality claim is about the match between an augmentation and the shift it faces, not about photometric augmentation in general. Our image statistics pool whole frames, which dark background dominates, so object-masked statistics would test the mechanism more directly. Finally, our conformal coverage is marginal, and Sec. 9 shows how far it is from conditional. Future work. The mechanism suggests its own tests: augmentation that models sunlamps actual structure (specular highlights, hard shadows, saturation clipping), full fine-tuning, and weighted conformal prediction [26]. The last needs density ratios between domains that barely overlap, which is exactly what sim-to-real lacks. For fields that must rely on synthetic data, the question to ask of robustness intervention is not how much does it help? but which way does it push the training distribution?, and uncertainty has to be validated under the shift, or wrong pose arrives wrapped in confident interval.

It anchors near chance to predictor one could actually build, rather than to an assumption about the distribution. The constant is fitted on the 28,000 training labels only. Fitting it on test domain would make it an oracle rather than baseline, so neither real domain enters the estimate. For rotation we take the principal eigenvector of = (cid:80) , which minimises chordal distance and is unaffected by the quaternion double cover. We then refine it with five Karcher iterations on the sphere: sign-align each qi to the current mean, log-map into the tangent space, average, and exp-map back. The SO(3) geodesic distance is twice the S3 one, so iterating on the sphere targets the same minimiser as our reported metric. sections.content: Code, results and predictions. Everything is in the public repository, https://github.com/ lokindoo/spacecraft-pose-estimation. The tag arxiv-v1 reproduces this version, and the tag sim2science-2026-camera-ready the workshop version. Zenodo archives every tag under doi:10.5281/zenodo.24011140, which lists each version, and the workshop version alone under doi:10.5281/zenodo.24011141. Each tag holds its papers source, with script that checks every number in the paper against the repositorys results/. Per-image predictions for all 20 runs behind the tables are released as CSV, so new metric needs neither the data pipeline nor GPU. Runs. Configurations, seeds and the selection rule are as in Sec. 3. The eight published runs (seed 42 of both frozen arms, and all six layer-4 runs) were trained on free-tier Colab GPU. Frozen augmented seeds 43 and 44, ablation arms and (three seeds each) and the control were trained with the released package on an Apple M5 GPU. The frozen-backbone heads were trained on cached features on the same machines CPU, in minutes each. On Colab 20-epoch run took about 1.8 for the frozen un-augmented arm and 2.02.3 for the layer-4 un-augmented arm. With augmentation, epochs took about 790 s, some 4.4 per run, whether or not the backbone was frozen. On the M5 most runs took 3.14.2 h, and two arm-A runs took about 14 of wall-clock time. head on cached features trains in about 2.5 minutes. Checkpoints. results/checkpoints.json records, for each of the 17 trained checkpoints, its configuration, seed, selected epoch, hardware and sha256. The weights are on Zenodo with model card, under CC BY 4.0: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24140385. Software. requirements.txt pins the versions the pipeline was written against (PyTorch 2.13.0, torchvision 0.28.0). The M5 runs used Python 3.14.8, PyTorch 2.14.1 and torchvision 0.29.1, frozen in requirements-m5.txt. The Colab runs used the Colab image of July 2026, whose versions were not recorded. The control rerun (Sec. 6) bounds what hardware and software together moved seed 42, and none of the 81 unit tests needs data.
